title: Reading a tide table and a current table
teaches: Planning a beach walk at a minus tide and a crossing at slack water
summary: **A tide table lists the turns.** Each high and low, with its time and its height in feet above a fixed zero.
**Zero is the average lower low.** Mean lower low water (MLLW) is the average of each day's lower low over 19 years, so on about half of all days the lower low falls below it.
**A minus tide is below that average.** On a flat low-tide terrace each foot below zero uncovers a strip of beach many metres wide.
**Charts use the same zero.** A charted depth plus the table's height gives the depth now; the water is shallower than charted only during minus tides, and then by a few feet at most.
**The rule of twelfths estimates the height between turns.** In six equal parts of the time the water moves 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the range.
**A current table lists slack, maximum flood and maximum ebb.** Speeds are in knots, and one knot is about half a metre a second.
**Slack in a narrows comes after high water.** At Deception Pass it can be an hour or more late, so a crossing is planned from the current table.
**Slack in a fast pass is short.** Around the biggest slacks the water runs under a knot for well under an hour; in a slow inlet, for two hours or more.
**Seattle's daytime minus tides come from late spring to midsummer.** For a fixed hour, pick the day with the lowest water in that hour, not the lowest number in the week.

blocks.text: At Constellation Park, on the West Seattle shore just south of Alki Point, a broad shelf of rock and cobble runs out under the Sound. On most days the water covers its outer edge. On a few days each spring and summer the water draws back far enough to bare the whole shelf, and people walk out among the pools to find sea stars, anemones and crabs that spend nearly all their lives under water. The days and the minutes when that happens are published more than a year ahead.

They come from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA), the federal agency that, among much else, predicts the tides and currents of every American coast. This lesson reads two of its tables and plans by them. The first target is a walk at a **minus tide**, at noon on a day you are free. The second is the moment the current under the Deception Pass bridge stops, which a different table gives. Lessons 8 to 11 explained why the water rises, falls and runs as it does: the two daily bulges (lesson 8), the unequal lows (lesson 9), the tide as a wave in the basin (lesson 10) and the current through a narrows (lesson 11). Here the tables do the predicting, and the skill is reading them.

blocks.text: The real tables are on NOAA's Tides and Currents site, tidesandcurrents.noaa.gov. Search for Seattle, or for its station number, 9447130: the tide station on the downtown waterfront whose records, going back to 1898, the predictions are computed from. Ask for a month of predictions and set the time to local time (marked LST/LDT), or in summer every entry will be an hour away from your clock. You get a list: for each day, the times of the highs and lows and how high each will be, in feet and in centimetres, each marked H or L. Together the highs and lows are the **turns** of the tide.

A late-May day reads something like this: 04:09 H 13.0, 11:22 L −2.1, 18:09 H 9.5, 23:03 L 5.2. That day, a Saturday, comes from a made-up week used through this lesson, in the text and in every figure. It is built the way NOAA builds its own predictions, as a sum of regular waves (lesson 9), so it looks like a real table, but for a real walk look up the real one.

Seattle's tide is mixed, as lesson 9 explained: two highs and two lows a day, of unequal size. The higher of the two highs is the **higher high** and the lower of the two lows the **lower low**. The table shows the inequality at a glance: the morning high is 13 feet, the evening high under 10, and one low is far below the other.

Every height is measured from a fixed zero called the **datum**. For tides in the United States the zero is **mean lower low water**, MLLW. Take each day's lower low, collect them over 19 years,[^epoch] and average them: that average is zero. So zero is not the bottom of the tide. It is the middle of all the lower lows, and on about half of all days the lower low falls below it. Those are the minus tides, printed with a minus sign: −2.1 ft is 2.1 feet (64 cm) below the average lower low. At Seattle the average higher high stands about 11.4 ft (3.5 m) above zero, the biggest highs of the year reach 13 or 14 ft, and the lowest lows of the year fall about 3 to 4 ft below zero.

Why measure from a low level and not from the middle? Because the same zero is used under the water. The depths on a nautical chart of Puget Sound are measured down from MLLW, so a sailor adds the table's height to the charted depth to get the depth now. For most of every day the tide is above zero and the water is deeper than the chart says. Only during a minus tide is it shallower, and then by a few feet at most, which the table announces with its minus sign.[^chart]

What a minus tide is worth depends on the beach. Many of the Sound's beaches have a steep upper part of gravel and cobble and, below it, a broad, nearly flat shelf, the **low-tide terrace**. On a steep slope a foot of height is only a short distance along the ground, so while the tide falls across the upper beach the water's edge hardly moves. On the flat terrace a foot of height is a long way across, and every foot uncovers a wide strip.

blocks.caption: A model beach, with heights in feet above MLLW: a steep upper beach and a flat low-tide terrace. The bar at the bottom measures how far the water's edge stands from where it stands at an average higher high.
blocks.task: Guess how much beach the lower fall uncovers, then take the tide down to a minus tide

blocks.text: On this model beach the strip between a −1 ft and a −3 ft tide is about 40 m wide, and the animals that live on the outer terrace are uncovered only on the few lowest tides of the year. That is why people who walk the shore care about tenths of a foot below zero.

A tide table lists only the turns. Between them the water does not fall at an even pace. It starts slowly just after high water, runs fastest in the middle, and slows again as it nears the low, the way a swing slows at each end of its arc. Sailors estimate the height between the turns with the **rule of twelfths**. The **range** is the difference in height between a high and the low after it (or a low and the high after it). Split the time between them into six equal parts, and in those parts the water falls 1, 2, 3, 3, 2 and 1 twelfths of the range.

Take Saturday's big fall: 13.0 ft at 04:09 to −2.1 ft at 11:22. The range is 13.0 − (−2.1) = 15.1 ft, so a twelfth is about 1.26 ft. The time between is 7 hours 13 minutes, so a sixth is about 72 minutes. By 07:45, three sixths in, the water has fallen 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 twelfths, half the range, to about 5.5 ft. By 10:10, five sixths in, it has fallen 11 twelfths, to about −0.8 ft. The last 72 minutes bring only the final twelfth, a little over a foot.

blocks.caption: Saturday's tide in the model, the four entries of its table, and the rule of twelfths drawn between them.
blocks.task: Find the time when the water falls fastest

blocks.text: For a walk this matters in two ways. The last sixth before the low and the first sixth after it each bring only a twelfth of the range, so on a day like Saturday the water stays within about a foot of its lowest for roughly an hour either side of the low. Reaching the beach an hour before low water loses you little. And the middle hours of the rising tide come back fast: on Saturday afternoon the water climbs more than a foot every half hour, over a terrace where a foot of height is many metres of beach.

The rule assumes each fall and rise is shaped like the others, slow, fast, slow, and the same either side of its middle. Seattle's are not quite that. The real curve can be flatter near one turn than the other, most of all in the small evening rise and fall, and there the rule drifts off by up to half a foot. For planning a walk that is close enough. For taking a deep boat over a shoal it is not, and NOAA also gives its predictions at six-minute intervals, which trace the curve itself, the line the figures here draw from the model.

A tide table says how high the water stands. A **current table** says how fast it moves, and which way, at one place: Deception Pass, Admiralty Inlet, the Tacoma Narrows, Rich Passage. NOAA's Tides and Currents site lists these too, under current predictions. For each day the table gives the times of **slack water**, when the current stops and turns, and between each pair of slacks the time and speed of the strongest current: **maximum flood**, running in from the sea, and **maximum ebb**, running out. Speeds are in **knots**: a knot is one nautical mile an hour,[^knot] about 1.85 km/h or half a metre a second, a slow walk. Ebb speeds are often printed with a minus sign.

Deception Pass is the narrow gap between Whidbey Island and Fidalgo Island, at the north end of Whidbey, with a high bridge across it. The flood runs east through it, from Rosario Strait into Skagit Bay, and the ebb runs west. On the biggest tides the current peaks at 6 to 8 knots, faster than a kayaker can paddle, and the water below the bridge breaks into whirlpools and standing waves. On an ordinary day it may peak at 4 or 5 knots. In a pass like this the water is moving almost all the time, and the table's slacks are short breaks in it.

blocks.caption: Deception Pass, between Whidbey and Fidalgo Islands. On the flood the water runs east through the gap from Rosario Strait toward Skagit Bay; on the ebb, west.

blocks.text: Look at when the slacks come. Lesson 11 explained why, in a narrows, the current keeps running after the tide outside reaches its high: the current follows the difference in level between the two sides, and the basin inside is still lower, still filling, when the water outside has peaked. Slack at Deception Pass can come an hour or more after high water at the nearest tide station. That is why the current is predicted for the pass itself and printed in its own table: the height of the tide nearby does not tell you when the water in the pass will stop.

blocks.caption: Saturday in the model: the tide outside, the current it drives in a fast pass (Deception Pass) or in a wide, slow inlet, and the current table that results. Flood is up, ebb down; dots mark the slacks, and the shaded band is slower than 1 knot.
blocks.task: Guess how long the slow water lasts, then find a slack in each of the two channels

blocks.text: In a fast pass the slack is short. A flood and the ebb after it take about twelve and a half hours together, so the current swings from about 7 knots one way to 7 knots the other in some six hours. It passes through the slow speeds quickly, and around the biggest slacks it runs under a knot for well under an hour. In a wide inlet where the current peaks at 2 or 3 knots, the slow water lasts two hours or more. Divers, kayakers and boats with small engines plan around the slack windows of the passes and are ready to go before the predicted slack, since wind and a river in flood can move the real slack away from the predicted one.

**Watching it stop.** Look up the Deception Pass current predictions for a day with a big tide. Park in one of the state park's lots near either end of the bridge (they ask for a Washington Discover Pass), walk out on the bridge's walkway, and keep off the roadway, which is narrow and busy. Stand there at the time of maximum current and watch the water: whirlpools, standing waves and a sharp line where fast water meets slow. Then come back to the bridge at the slack the table gives. The swirls fade and the surface goes smooth, and within the next half hour the floating weed and foam begin to drift the other way.

Back to the beach. Seattle's lowest tides come near the new and full moon (lesson 8), and the lower low of each day is deepest when the Moon stands far north or south of the equator, its high **declination** (lesson 9). Which of the day's two lows is the lower one, and so when it falls, also depends on the Sun's share of the daily tide, and that changes with the seasons (lesson 9 again). In late spring and early summer the lower low comes around the middle of the day; in winter, lows just as deep come in the middle of the night. So the year's best beach walks fall between about late April and July, in runs of several days around the new and full moons.

Within a run, the low comes later each day, by about 50 minutes on average, while its depth grows to a peak and shrinks again. The deepest low of the run is not always the best one. If your free hour is fixed, the day to pick is the one with the lowest water in that hour. A day whose low falls an hour or two before your hour has already risen by then, and the rule of twelfths says by how much.

blocks.caption: The made-up week of Seattle predictions in late May, Saturday among them. Minus tides are in bold. The day's curve appears once you have guessed.
blocks.task: Guess which day has the lowest water during the free hour, then step through the week

blocks.text: Thursday has the week's lowest low, −2.7 ft, but at 09:55, and by noon the water has risen to about the zero line. Friday's low, −2.6 ft at 10:38, is deeper than Saturday's but comes earlier, so by noon on Friday the water has risen more than a foot. Saturday's −2.1 ft comes at 11:22, only 38 minutes before noon. The rule of twelfths puts the water at about −1.6 ft at noon; the model's curve, flatter at the bottom than the rule assumes, says −1.8. Either way it is the lowest of the week in that hour.

Good places for a minus-tide walk in Seattle include Constellation Park and Lincoln Park in West Seattle and the North Beach of Discovery Park, below the bluffs north of West Point.[^subordinate] On the lowest tides each uncovers rock, sand and pools that are under water most of the year. Constellation Park has street parking along Beach Drive; Lincoln Park and Discovery Park have car parks above the beach and a walk down a path, a longer one at Discovery Park. In many summers the Seattle Aquarium sends volunteer beach naturalists to some Seattle beaches on the lowest tides; its website lists the days when it does.

The animals on the outer terrace are in the air for a few hours a year. Walk on bare rock and sand where you can, turn any rock you lift back the way it lay, and leave animals where you find them. Keep an eye on the time too. The flood comes back fastest in its middle hours, and over a flat terrace the water can fill a low channel behind you and leave you on a bank cut off from the shore. Plan to be back off the outer terrace within about an hour after the predicted low.

blocks.caption: Six questions on reading the tables
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A Seattle tide table lists a low of −2.5 ft. What does the minus sign mean?
choices: The water will stand 2.5 ft below the average of each day's lower low, uncovering extra beach
The water will stand 2.5 ft below mean sea level, the height halfway between high and low tide
The water will stand 2.5 ft below the lowest level ever recorded at the Seattle tide station
items.why: Heights are measured from mean lower low water, the average of each day's lower low. A minus tide is lower than that average, which happens on about half of all days.

items.ask: Why is the zero of a US tide table set at the average lower low rather than at mean sea level?
choices: Charts measure depths from it, so the water is at least as deep as charted except during minus tides
It is the lowest level the tide can reach, so a table never needs to print a negative height
It is the level where the tide spends most of its time, so heights near zero are the most common
items.why: With depths and tides measured from the same low zero, charted depth plus the table's height gives the depth now, and the chart overstates the depth only on minus tides, by a few feet at most.

items.ask: High water is 12 ft at 06:00 and low water 0 ft at 12:00. By the rule of twelfths, about how high is the tide at 08:00?
choices: About 9 ft: the first two sixths of the time bring 1 + 2 twelfths of the 12 ft fall
About 8 ft: the water falls an even 2 ft in each of the six hours between the turns
About 7 ft: the first two sixths bring 2 + 3 twelfths, since a fall starts fastest
items.why: In the first two sixths the water falls 1 + 2 = 3 twelfths of 12 ft, so 3 ft, leaving about 9 ft. It falls slowly just after the turn.

items.ask: High water at the tide station nearest Deception Pass is at 10:40. How should a kayaker time a trip through the pass?
choices: By the slack in the pass's own current table, which there often comes over an hour after 10:40
At 10:40 itself, since in a narrows the current stops at the moment the water outside peaks
About an hour before 10:40, since the current in a narrows turns before the tide outside peaks
items.why: In a narrows the current follows the difference in level between the two sides, so it keeps running after high water outside. The current table for the pass gives the slack.

items.ask: Why does Deception Pass run under 1 knot for a much shorter time around slack than a wide inlet with weak currents does?
choices: Its current swings from about 7 knots one way to 7 the other in six hours, so it passes the slow speeds fast
Its narrow gap funnels the wind, which pushes the water through and keeps the current from stopping for long
Its water is deep, so friction with the bed is too weak to hold the current back as it nears the turn
items.why: The faster the current at its peak, the faster it changes through zero. In the model, a 7 knot pass runs under 1 knot for well under an hour; a 2 to 3 knot inlet for two hours or more.

items.ask: Why are late spring and early summer the season for minus-tide walks at Seattle?
choices: The day's lower low then falls near midday, while in winter lows just as deep fall at night
The Sun's pull is strongest then, so the summer lows are much deeper than the winter ones
The Moon is nearest the Earth then, so the deepest lows of the year all come in those months
items.why: Deep lows happen all year, but which of the two daily lows is the lower one, and so when it falls, changes with the season. In late spring and summer it is the daytime low.

epoch.title: Why 19 years
epoch.text: The tilt of the Moon's orbit to the Earth's equator swings through a cycle of 18.6 years, and the sizes of the tides swing with it. Averaging over a whole cycle makes the zero the same whichever years are chosen, apart from changes in sea level itself. As the sea rises NOAA recomputes its datums from a newer run of years, so zero on the table moves slightly from one recomputation to the next.

chart.title: Other zeros
chart.text: Not every country uses the average lower low. British charts use the lowest astronomical tide, about the lowest level the tide reaches in ordinary weather, so a minus height almost never appears. Canadian charts of the Salish Sea use a low datum of their own, so a Canadian and an American table for nearby places can give different numbers for the same water.

knot.title: The knot
knot.text: Sailors once measured speed by throwing a wooden board over the stern on a line with knots tied in it at even spacings, and counting how many knots ran out while a small sandglass, like an egg timer, emptied. The spacing and the glass were matched so that the count gave nautical miles an hour. A nautical mile is 1,852 m, about one minute of latitude.

subordinate.title: Beaches without a station
subordinate.text: NOAA keeps long-running tide stations at a few places, such as Seattle and Port Townsend, and gives many more places as differences from one of them: add so many minutes to the times and scale the heights by so much. For a beach a few miles from the Seattle station the differences are small, so the Seattle table serves well.
